title: Two Pixels, One New Name
concept: NOAA's Alaska Fisheries Science Center page on its research tools, last updated November 6th, now calls its seal and polar bear detectors and its ear stone aging tool super intelligence. NOAA survey planes shoot color and thermal photos together from 1,000 feet, a seal can be as small as two pixels, a million images may hold 7,000 to 9,000 animals, and finding them by hand took a year. NOAA's own 2019 article calls the same seal work artificial intelligence. A September 29th executive order told agencies to say super intelligence instead, and for now defines it as what the law already calls artificial intelligence, with a proposed new definition due November 28th. The order's case and a procurement law dean's doubt get equal signs on one floe, the page gives no accuracy figure, and the film ends on the same two pixels it opened on.

divergence_note: The last films were a brass faucet on an overcast pewter-sage gravel lot (11-13), a flagging-orange stake tag on raven polar dusk (11-12), a roof puck in pink-gold ice fog (11-11) and a vermilion take-a-number machine on a violet shore (11-10). This film is high-noon white pack ice with cobalt leads, a thermal violet survey view and gold leaf on exactly one nameplate. Its hero is a living animal, a ringed seal, not an object, its AI presence is a twin-lens survey camera, its device is a zoom through two pixels and a plate that grows while the lenses never change, and its test is two identical signs on one floe. Honest overlaps: 11-12 also had blue-white snow with blue shadow planes, answered here by a high-key noon sky and cobalt leads in every exterior. 11-10 had a violet shore, and violet here lives only inside the thermal frames. Shots 6 and 12 share the under-wing set as a deliberate callback.

treatment.title: Two Pixels, One New Name
treatment.summary: Explainer winner 'Two Pixels, One New Name' with grafts: a two-pixel thermal seal is the cold open and the button; the survey camera pod's riveted nameplate is the throughline; the color and thermal frames slide into register as the mechanism cutaway; Act 3 is two identical signposts frozen into one floe with the pod dead center.
treatment.judge_reasoning: Explainer pitch won (48 of 60): the only pitch that draws the mechanism, c21 lands on the act boundary, both loops legal with margin, Act 3 gives c20 and c23 identical size and light and the turn refuses to pick a side. Grafts: B's stamp that leaves machine learning showing (cut for length, c24 kept off screen), A's plate that grows while the lens keeps its size, A's sweating microscope and the ONE OF THESE IS A SEAL tile, D's seal watching both signs, D's puzzled glance, B's seal looking up at the lens in the button.

angle.thesis: Alaska's seal finder didn't get smarter on November 6th, it got a bigger name: by the order's own definition 'super intelligence' means exactly what the law calls artificial intelligence, and the real feat, finding two-pixel seals and reading ear stones ten times faster than a microscope, never needed the promotion.
supporting_facts: The page now says super intelligence for the seal, polar bear and otolith tools (c2, c3, c10, c12), while NOAA's own 2019 and 2024 articles about the same work say artificial intelligence and deep learning (c11, c15), and GAIA states its former name outright (c16, c17).

Sec. 3(a) defines Super Intelligence as the technologies covered by the statutory definition of artificial intelligence (c21), and the page backs the new word with no new capability claim: seal detection still 'developed', aging still 'could revolutionize', no accuracy figure anywhere (c3, c14, c26).

The capability is real and Alaskan: seals as small as two pixels (c8) in millions of color and thermal images (c5, c6), 7,000 to 9,000 animals per million images (c7), a year of hand search after each season before automation (c9), ear stones in 30 to 50 seconds, more than ten times faster than a microscope (c13, c14).
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: The administration's own case, in its own words: these systems 'increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era' (c20), and the order asks for a capability-based federal definition by November 28th (c22). A name built for ambition is a legitimate policy choice, and an agency page that follows a lawful directive is doing its job. Tillipman's 'no purpose other than rebranding' (c23) is shown at equal weight, attributed. The film takes no side on the politics; the tools are the constant across both views. November 28th is the closing open question, not the thesis.
angle.falsifier: False today if the order gives SI any operative meaning beyond 15 U.S.C. 9401(3) (c21), or if the updated page backs the new term with capability evidence (accuracy figures, new tasks) the 2019 and 2024 NOAA articles didn't have (c26, c11, c15). Could become false on November 28th if the proposed definition sets a bar these tools fail.
angle.second_movement: Act two turns on c21: the order that renamed everything defines the new word as the old legal one, machine learning still sits in the page heading (c24), and GAIA kept its letters while changing what they stand for (c17). Act four turns forward: a definition due November 28th that doesn't exist yet (c22).
runner_ups: A (enthusiast) pure wonder at the tools: kept as Act 1 and the button, rejected as thesis because it ignores the definition.
B (skeptic) cost to public clarity: withdrawn in cross-challenge, no claim shows anyone confused; kept only as the observable two-names inconsistency.
C (contrarian) the name moved before the definition, Nov 28 decides: conceded its falsifier may not be checkable while the film is live; kept as the closing open question.
guardrails: never quote the AFSC page's old wording, no archived copy (verdict)
never 'every mention was replaced', machine learning survives (c24)
the page names no order; say the order requires it and the page now says it
30 to 50 seconds is fish, never rockfish (c13)
millions of images collected, not processed (c5)
a year by hand was BEFORE automation, 2019 article, past tense (c9); never claim the year is now automated to a given speed
no accuracy figure on the page (c26), say 'the page gives no accuracy figure'
GAIA is Northeast plus Alaska centers, not Alaska-only (c16)
Nov 28 is proposed legislative language to the President, not law, not yet written (c22)
no Trump 'artificial anything' quote, no Navy memo, no Truth Social post
no mockery of the order or the President; c20 gets a straight scene

open_loop.what: Which tile is the seal? Planted as ONE OF THESE IS A SEAL on a dark tile in the million-tile wall, reminded when the 2019 article's seal photo wears the same pin tag, paid when the camera cranes into that same tagged tile and the seal rises out of it to look up at the lens.

open_loop_2.what: Did it get smarter? Planted as the pod glancing down at its new gold plate under DID IT GET SMARTER, paid when the accuracy tag swings down blank, the detector box finds nothing to box and the pod looks up at its own plate under NOTHING ON THE PAGE SHOWS SMARTER.
